To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the nuclease domain in the amino terminal region of Escherichian coli polymerase I is a functional homologue to the yeast FEN-1 and the human flap endonuclesse 1 (Fen-1).
the N-terminal domain of DNA polymerase I from E. coli encodes a functional FEN-1 nuclease.
we have shown the Escherichia coli polymerase I nuclease domain encodes a functional flap endonuclesse homologue.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of DNA polymerases in genome maintenance and repair.
the molecular basis for the suppression of phenotypes associated with the absence of the FEN- 1 homologue in yeast by a nuclease domain encoded within the DNA polymerase of E. coli.
the identification and characterization of a new class of DNA polymerases that are involved in DNA replication and repair.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the N-terminal domain of PolN encodes a functional nuclease that suppresses the phenotypes of the rad27 null strain in S. cerevisiae.
the N-terminal domain of E. coli polymerase I is a functional homologue to FEN-1, and overexpression of this domain can suppress phenotypes of a rad27 null mutant.
the N- terminal domain of E. coli DNA polymerase I encloses a functional FEN-1 nuclease that can partially suppress the phenotypes associated with the deletion of the S. cerevisiae RAD27 gene.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the N-terminal domain of E. coli DNA PolI is a functional homologue for S. cerevisiae FEN-1/Rad27.
the nuclease domain in E. coli DNA polymerase 1 can functionally substitute for the nuclease function of the yeast Rad27 protein.
PolN can substitute for Rad27, but that the PolN-Rad27 differences in activity may explain the partial suppression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PolI is a multifunctional enzyme that can carry out both DNA replication and repair.
the nuclease domain in PolN is sufficient to suppress the phenotypes associated with the rad27 null mutation.
the N-terminal region, which is highly conserved among bacterial DNA polymerases, contains an active nuclease domain that is capable of suppressing some phenotypes of a FEN-1 null mutant.
